The name is derived from <Avestan> [*Harā Bərəzaitī*](Hara_Berezaiti "Hara Berezaiti"), a legendary mountain in [Iranian mythology](Persian_mythology "Persian mythology"). *Harā Bərəzaitī* reflects [Proto-Iranian](Proto-Iranian_language "Proto-Iranian language") **Harā Bṛzatī*, which was reformed into [Middle Persian](Middle_Persian "Middle Persian") as *Harborz*, and into Modern Persian as *Alborz*.[[8]](Mount_Elbrus#cite_note-alborziranica-9) *Bṛzatī* is the feminine form of the adjective **bṛzant* ("high"), the reconstructed ancestor of [Modern Ossetian](Ossetian_language "Ossetian language") *bærzond* ("high", "peak"), [Modern Persian](Persian_language "Persian language") *barz* ("high"), *berāzande* ("elegant"), and *boland* ("high", "tall"),[[8]](Mount_Elbrus#cite_note-alborziranica-9) and [Modern Kurdish](Kurdish_language "Kurdish language") *barz* ("high"). *Harā* may be interpreted as "watch" or "guard", from [Indo-European](Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages") **ser* ("protect").[[8]](Mount_Elbrus#cite_note-alborziranica-9) <Circassians> use the name "Uash-ha Makhua" which means "The mountain of happiness", The name "Mingi Taw" used by <Karachays> and <Balkars> means "Eternal Mountain" in [Turkic languages](Turkic_languages "Turkic languages").[[10]](Mount_Elbrus#cite_note-11)

Elbrus is situated in the northwest of the <Caucasus>, 100 kilometres from the [Black Sea](Black_Sea "Black Sea") and 370 kilometres from the [Caspian Sea](Caspian_Sea "Caspian Sea"), which is visible from Elbrus on exceptionally clear days.[[11]](Mount_Elbrus#cite_note-Tomb-NYT-12) It rises 5,642 metres above the sea level. Located eleven kilometres north of the [Greater Caucasus Watershed](Greater_Caucasus#Watershed "Greater Caucasus"), marking the border with [Georgia](Georgia_(country) "Georgia (country)"), it is on the border of the Russian republics of <Kabardino-Balkaria> and <Karachay-Cherkessia>. It is the highest peak in both Russia and Europe.[[12]](Mount_Elbrus#cite_note-13)

**Puncak Jaya** ( Indonesian: [ˈpuntʃak ˈdʒaja]; literally "Glorious Peak"), ([Amungme](Amung_people "Amung people"): **Nemangkawi Ninggok**)[[2]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-2) or **Carstensz Pyramid** (/ˈkɑːrstəns/) on the island of [New Guinea](New_Guinea "New Guinea"), with an elevation of 4,884 m (16,024 ft), is the [highest mountain peak of an island](List_of_islands_by_highest_point "List of islands by highest point") on Earth. The mountain is located in the [Sudirman Range](Sudirman_Range "Sudirman Range") of the highlands of [Mimika Regency](Mimika_Regency "Mimika Regency"), [Central Papua](Central_Papua "Central Papua"), <Indonesia>.

The massive, open cut [Grasberg](Grasberg_mine "Grasberg mine") gold and copper mine, the world's [fifth-largest gold mine](List_of_largest_gold_mines_by_production "List of largest gold mines by production"), is 4 km (2.5 mi) west of Puncak Jaya.

Other summits are *[East Carstensz Peak](Carstensz_East "Carstensz East")* (4,808 m [15,774 ft]), *<Sumantri>* (4,870 m [15,980 ft]) and *[Ngga Pulu](Ngga_Pulu "Ngga Pulu")* (4,863 m [15,955 ft]). Other names include **Nemangkawi** in the [Amungkal](Amung_language "Amung language") language, **Carstensz Toppen** and **Gunung Soekarno**.[[3]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-VAS-Si-Lj-3) It is also the highest point between the <Himalayas> and the <Andes>. Some sources claim Papua New Guinea's [Mt Wilhelm](Mount_Wilhelm "Mount Wilhelm"), 4,509 m (14,793 ft), as the highest mountain peak in <Oceania>, on account of Indonesia being part of Asia (Southeast Asia).[[4]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-4)

## Etymology

The name of the mountain in the indigenous [Amungme](Amung_people "Amung people") peoples' language is Nemangkawi Ninggok meaning Peak of the White Arrow. The name Puncak Jaya is [Indonesian](Indonesian_language "Indonesian language") for 'Glorious Peak'. It is also known as Carstensz Pyramid, Mount Jayawijaya, or Mount Carstensz.

## History

The highlands surrounding the peak were inhabited before European contact, and the peak is known as **Nemangkawi** in [Amungkal](Amung_language "Amung language").

## Dutch discovery

Puncak Jaya was named "Carstensz Pyramid" after [Dutch](Dutch_Republic "Dutch Republic") explorer [Jan Carstenszoon](Jan_Carstenszoon "Jan Carstenszoon"), who was the first [European](Europe "Europe") who sighted the [glaciers](Glacier "Glacier") on the peak of the mountain on a rare clear day in 1623.[[5]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-5) The sighting went unverified for over two centuries, and Carstensz was ridiculed in Europe when he said he had seen snow near the equator. It appeared on maps of the time as *Sneebergh.*[[6]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-6)

The [snowfield](Snowfield "Snowfield") of Puncak Trikora, 170 km (106 mi) east of here, was reached as early as 1909 by a Dutch explorer, [Hendrik Albert Lorentz](Hendrik_Albert_Lorentz "Hendrik Albert Lorentz") with six of his [Dayak](Dayak_people "Dayak people") [Kenyah](Kenyah_people "Kenyah people") porters recruited from the Apo Kayan in <Borneo>.[[7]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-7) The predecessor of the [Lorentz National Park](Lorentz_National_Park "Lorentz National Park"), which encompasses the Carstensz Range, was established in 1919 following the report of this expedition.

### Climbing history

In 1936, the Dutch [Carstensz Expedition](Carstensz_Expedition "Carstensz Expedition"), unable to establish definitively which of the three summits was the highest, attempted to climb each. [Anton Colijn](Anton_Colijn "Anton Colijn"), [Jean Jacques Dozy](Jean_Jacques_Dozy "Jean Jacques Dozy") and Frits Wissel reached both the glacier-covered East Carstensz and Ngga Pulu summits on December 5, but, due to bad weather, failed in their attempts to climb the bare Carstensz Pyramid. Because of extensive snow melt, Ngga Pulu has become a 4,862 m (15,951 ft) subsidiary peak, but it has been estimated that in 1936 (when glaciers still covered 13 km2 (5.0 sq mi) of the mountain; see map) Ngga Pulu was indeed the highest summit, reaching over 4,900 m (16,100 ft).[[8]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-8)

The now-highest Carstensz Pyramid summit was not climbed until 1962, by an expedition led by the Austrian mountaineer [Heinrich Harrer](Heinrich_Harrer "Heinrich Harrer") (of *[Seven Years in Tibet](Seven_Years_in_Tibet "Seven Years in Tibet")* fame, and climber of the <Eiger> North Face) with three other expedition members – the New Zealand mountaineer [Philip Temple](Philip_Temple "Philip Temple"), the Australian rock climber Russell Kippax, and the Dutch patrol officer Albertus (Bert) Huizenga. Temple had previously led an expedition into the area and pioneered the access route to the mountains.[[9]](Puncak_Jaya#cite_note-9)

When Indonesia took control of the province in 1963, the peak was renamed Poentja' Soekarno (Simplified [Indonesian](Indonesian_language "Indonesian language"): Puncak Sukar

After climbing Hannel’s Spur, the peak now named [Mount Townsend](Mount_Townsend_(Snowy_Mountains) "Mount Townsend (Snowy Mountains)") was reached. Here Strzelecki used his instruments to make observations. Mt Townsend is Australia's second highest mountain, adjacent to and almost the same height as Mt Kosciuszko, and Strzelecki saw that the neighbouring peak was slightly higher. In the presence of Macarthur he named the higher summit Mount Kosciusko after the famous Polish-Lithuanian military leader who died in 1817.
